Home Paid news feed Foto Agerpres Press Monitoring Bucharest Phone: +4 021.2076.110 Interim ForMin Toiu informs EU counterparts about illegal incursions by Russian drones into national airspace Category: English Date: 2026-09-03 13:10:11 Foto: GRIGORE POPESCU / AGERPRES FOTO Interim Foreign Minister Oana Toiu informed her EU counterparts about repeated illegal incursions by Russian drones into Romania's national airspace and exclusive economic zone and stressed the need for enhanced measures to protect the Eastern Flank, taking into account the complementarity of EU and NATO instruments. Oana Toiu attended the informal meeting of EU foreign ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, on Tuesday and Wednesday, with Ireland holding the Presidency of the EU Council. According to a Foreign Ministry press release sent to AGERPRES on Thursday, the first session, which also invited ministers from Canada, Switzerland, Iceland, Norway, the United Kingdom and Ukraine to join the discussion, addressed the response to Russia's aggression against Ukraine and the escalation of the conflict, including in the context of the expansion of security incidents in the Black Sea and the findings of the German authorities concerning the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Oana Toiu stressed that the security situation in the Black Sea as a result of Russia's aggression has a major impact on grain exports, global food security and grain prices. 'Romania is closely coordinating with the Republic of Moldova, Ukraine and the European Commission to facilitate grain exports and mitigate the challenges affecting their prices. She stressed the role of the Port of Constanta and the Solidarity Lanes in increasing grain transit to the Middle East and Africa and highlighted the need for measures to protect both the local market and local agricultural producers in the EU,' the Foreign Ministry release reads. Oana Toiu also informed her counterparts about repeated illegal incursions by Russian drones into Romania's national airspace and exclusive economic zone and stressed the need for enhanced measures to protect the Eastern Flank, taking into account the complementarity of EU and NATO instruments. 'She mentioned the intensification of Russia's hybrid actions against EU member states and partners, expressing solidarity with those affected and stressing the need for a coherent and coordinated approach to these actions. During the session on improving EU action in the area of Common Foreign and Security Policy/CFSP, Minister Oana Toiu highlighted Romania's joint efforts, together with other EU member states and the European External Action Service, to strengthen the EU's global profile, with an emphasis on making the most of the EU's strengths, unity and solidarity, while improving decision-making at European level,' the Foreign Ministry said. Such measures can produce results aimed at increasing trade and strengthening the partnerships needed for security and respect for international law, the source said. Oana Toiu highlighted the opportunities that the forthcoming UN General Assembly could provide for a joint EU effort to reform the UN and strengthen multilateralism, as well as for more effective coordination in support of European priorities. During the final session, dedicated to the situation in the Middle East, the focus was on supporting initiatives aimed at maritime security and freedom of navigation in compliance with international law. The Romanian minister pointed out that continued instability in the region is affecting supply chains and global energy prices. The Romanian official highlighted Romania's latest assistance to Gaza, with the organisation on 31 August of the 12th flight for the emergency medical evacuation of five paediatric patients. The operation directly reflects Romania's commitments under the Washington Board of Peace and confirms its efforts to support civilians severely affected by the humanitarian crisis in the Gaza Strip. https://www.dw.com/en/serbia-hope-tensio.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OZWQ Three days before a pivotal parliamentary election in Serbia, supporters of the Student List poured into central Belgrade for a final campaign rally Image: Marko Djurica/REUTERS Advertisement A sense of hope swept through Belgrade on Thursday evening as thousands gathered for the final rally of the Student List, the group of candidates put forward by the student movement that has been protesting against the government for almost exactly two years. The Student List is calling for an end to the current regime in Serbia via the ballot box in Sunday's parliamentary election . Many of those who attended the rally had spent days walking to the Serbian capital from all four corners of the country, turning the campaign finale into a display of solidarity and peaceful determination. "We have walked across Serbia from one end to the other, visited villages and neighborhoods, looked you in the eye and realized that we can count on you," biology student Arsa Stojanovic told the crowd. "People, it smells like freedom," added Aleksandar Cupic, professor of transport and traffic engineering, and a candidate on the Student List. Students emerge as agents of change After 24 months of protests sparked by the collapse of a concrete canopy at Novi Sad railway station , which killed 16 people in November 2024, Serbia is heading into an election unlike any other in the 14 years since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) first came to power. Three is the number of the Student List on the ballot paper Image: Armin Durgut/AP Photo/picture alliance For the first time in years, the ruling party faces a serious political challenge, which this time comes from a student movement that has channeled widespread public discontent into an electoral campaign. "These are the first elections since [Aleksandar] Vucic came to power in 2012 that are competitive and whose outcome is uncertain," political scientist Dusan Spasojevic told DW. "The student movement has generated hope among citizens and substantial support. Polls suggest that they could even win more than 40% of the vote." The Student List has framed the election as a chance to confront corruption and demand accountability for a disaster that became a symbol of institutional failure. In doing so, the students have sought to put aside the ideological, social and foreign-policy divisions that have long shaped Serbian politics. SNS presents itself as a guarantor of continuity Just a few kilometers away, also in Belgrade, the ruling SNS held its own final rally. 'They attacked us with billions of euros, and we defended ourselves with integrity, our program, love for our homeland and Serbia's achievements,' Aleksandar Vucic told his supporters on Thursday Image: AP Photo/picture alliance The message here was familiar: A vote for the SNS means stability, continuity and further prosperity, while a change of government would risk plunging the country into chaos. The party framed the election as a battle for Serbia's future and sovereignty, accusing its opponents of serving foreign interests. "They tried to destroy our country on foreign orders, and that is why this is the hardest battle," former President Aleksandar Vucic told his supporters. "They attacked us with billions of euros, and we defended ourselves with integrity, our program, love for our homeland and Serbia's achievements." Rising tension The campaign has increasingly been overshadowed by violence, reflecting a society in which political opponents are often portrayed not simply as rivals, but as enemies. It's not just students who support the Student List. The red hand became a symbol of the student protest movement in November 2024 Image: Uros Arsic/REUTERS By the final week of the campaign, CRTA, an independent election-monitoring organization, had recorded 116 incidents involving physical violence or verbal threats. The incidents included physical confrontations, attacks on campaigners and attempts to seize campaign banners. CRTA also reported that opposition activists, particularly those linked to the Student List, were also subjected to surveillance and police questioning. In some cases, the organization said, police were slow to protect opposition candidates and supporters. Allegations of links to criminal networks In the final runup to the election, there have also been a series of investigative reports examining alleged links between people connected to the ruling SNS and criminal networks. Published by independent media in the days before the election, the reports have brought renewed attention to questions of corruption, political influence and accountability — issues at the heart of the student movement's challenge to the government. But Spasojevic is skeptical that the revelations will make a significant difference to the election outcome. He argues that those who trust investigative media are likely to have already made up their minds, while voters who rely on pro-government outlets may never even see these reports. Concerns about irregularities There are also serious concerns about the fairness of the election process. The scandals that rocked Serbia and are shaping the election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video CRTA told DW that the election campaign has not been either free or fair from day one, citing "a narrowing of freedoms and deepening inequality" among candidates and voters. Its report found a pronounced imbalance in media coverage: Almost three-quarters of airtime devoted to political players on national television has featured government representatives, while more than 80% of coverage on the Student List has been negative. Ahead of the vote, the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN) published the testimony of a former member of the SNS, who described how public-sector employees were pressured to deliver votes for the party. DW has also learned from sources who want to remain anonymous that voters have been offered between €30 and €150 to vote for the SNS, with holiday packages reportedly offered to entire families if they pledge all their votes to the ruling party. What could come after the election? Many fear a period of turbulence, uncertainty and political crisis after the vote, with election night itself a particular source of anxiety. For weeks, the authorities have warned that students, allegedly with the help of foreign intelligence services, are preparing violence in the streets. In the final days of the campaign, several people were arrested on what the prosecution has said was the suspicion of plotting disturbances on election night. The best-case scenario, says Dusan Spasojevic, would be a decisive victory for one of the two opposing camps, leaving little room for the other to challenge the result. Supporters cheered Aleksandar Vucic and the ruling SNS party at a rally this week Image: Jelena Djukic Pejic/DW "But polls suggest that the margin will be narrow, and we will probably enter some kind of post-election crisis," he said, adding that a narrow victory for the ruling party would almost certainly be contested, given longstanding concerns about the fairness of the electoral process and allegations that some votes may have been obtained illegally. The EU's reaction could be crucial Whatever happens, the European Union 's response could be crucial. "I think the international response will be crucial in preventing major incidents and a further escalation of the crisis. It is the only thing that can persuade the authorities to accept defeat and refrain from an overly heavy-handed response to any protests or incidents," he told DW. An EU Commission spokesperson acknowledged to DW that key recommendations on improving Serbia's electoral framework remain unimplemented and also stressed that democracy and the rule of law are key to the accession process. Serbia has been an EU candidate country since 2012 . Back in Belgrade, the students ended their rally with a kolo , a traditional Serbian circle dance, projecting confidence in their chances at the ballot box. But the path to victory could prove difficult. The movement has vowed to defend every vote — setting the stage for a potentially tense election night if the results are disputed. The two machines address different aspects of sorting, from handling delicate blueberries to identifying internal fruit defects, Patrycja Urbańczuk, trade fair and marketing specialist of the company, explains. The blueberry sorter uses air pulses rather than mechanical mechanisms to remove fruit that does not meet the specified quality criteria. Urbańczuk describes the system and its inspection capabilities: "Our blueberry sorter featuring a pneumatic rejection system is one of the latest solutions in our portfolio. Instead of traditional mechanical mechanisms, fruit that does not meet the specified quality criteria is rejected using precise pulses of air, reducing direct mechanical contact with delicate blueberries. The system works in combination with an advanced vision system and stroboscopic lighting, enabling the detection of unripe fruit, discolouration and skin damage, among other defects. Compared with the previous model, the new machine also offers approximately 20-30% higher throughput." © Green Sort The sorter is scheduled to be demonstrated at Interpoma and ExpoSE. "The technology will be available to see live at the upcoming Interpoma and ExpoSE trade shows. These events will provide another opportunity to discover our solution and speak with the Green Sort team. We'll be able to demonstrate how the system works and present its capabilities in practice. We look forward to meeting industry professionals again and showcasing the results of our work." Green Sort has also completed testing of a new linear sorting machine, which Urbańczuk says is now being introduced to the market. It is the longest sorting line in the manufacturer's portfolio: "At the same time, we continue to develop our linear sorting solutions. We have just completed testing of our new sorting machine and are now introducing it to the market. It is the longest sorting line in our portfolio, marking another step forward in the development of Green Sort technology." "The key improvements include increased throughput and expanded quality control capabilities, including the detection of internal fruit damage," Urbańczuk continues. "This is another stage in the development of our technology, allowing us to better meet customer needs and quality requirements for sorted produce. The testing process allowed us to evaluate the machine's capabilities and prepare it for commercial launch. Expanding quality assessment to include internal damage provides an important addition to the sorting process. We believe that combining higher throughput with more detailed fruit inspection will offer significant value to our customers." © Nick Peters | FreshPlaza.com Green Sort's sorting equipment covers several fruit and vegetable categories. Urbańczuk outlines the company's current range and development priorities: "Our portfolio includes sorting solutions for blueberries, apples and other fruits, as well as selected vegetables such as potatoes, beetroot, peppers, tomatoes and onions. We continuously work to improve our existing machines and develop new features to expand sorting and automation capabilities. The completion of testing for our new linear sorting machine, together with preparations for upcoming trade shows, demonstrates that we are continuing to move forward. We monitor market needs and look for ways to further improve our solutions," she concludes. Ernie Poulson Submitted Photo Princess Catherine Caradja Submitted Photo Submitted Photo Submitted Photo Submitted Photo ❮ ❯ 🔊 Listen to this WILKES-BARRE — After his book “Devotion” became a movie, author Adam Makos said he went underground for three years to write “Tidal Wave,” which released Tuesday, Nov. 3. Makos, whose family is from Plymouth, said “Tidal Wave” has a unique connection to the Wyoming Valley — and he expects it to be his second book to be made into a movie. “Growing up, I read of the numerous men from Wilkes-Barre/Scranton who flew Operation Tidal Wave — the raid on Hitler’s Gas Station at Ploesti, Romania — and several who died on it,” Makos said. “It was America’s most daring, dramatic, and most highly decorated air mission in history.” Operation Tidal Wave was the most highly decorated and bloodiest air mission in history — 5 Medals of Honor, 56 Distinguished Service Crosses, and every man received the Distinguished Flying Cross. More Medals of Honor were awarded than for D-Day. “The Wyoming Valley had the most participants that I know of from this raid,” Makos said. “Growing up, we heard many of these stories at the Avoca air show and during interviews with local veterans. For the new book, we follow the raid from the cockpit for the first time ever. And then we follow what happened when our heroes got shot down and found unlikely allies — Romanian royalty.” Makos, 45, of Naples, Florida, has always drawn inspiration from the same person: his grandfather, Mike Makos, who flew heavy bombers at the tail end of World War II. ”I thought his service was remarkable — dropping boats from his B-17 to aircrews downed at sea,” Makos said. “He inspired me to learn more, and in every book I read there were stories about this famous singular raid against Hitler’s oil refineries — Operation Tidal Wave. I never imagined back then that I’d get to write a book that would bring the raid back to life. “That’s the ultimate reward. In 2026, we’re talking about the heroes of the past. They’re too important to ever forget.” In his book, “Devotion,” Makos told the inspirational story of the Navy’s most famous aviator duo — Lt. Tom Hudner and Ensign Jesse Brown — and the Marines they fought to defend. Makos, a writer, editor, historian and publisher, specializes in war novels and biographies. He appeared on the New York Times Best Seller list twice for his works “Spearhead” and “A Higher Call.” He also authored “Voices of the Pacific,” which follows Marines and seamen who served in the Pacific during World War II. Gallagher — Scranton • 2nd Lt. Charles A. Hoffman — Scranton • Tech. Sgt. Frederick H. Homnick — Wilkes-Barre • Tech. Sgt. Thomas A. Laskowski Jr. — Scranton, Aircraft: Wing and a Prayer Locals killed at Ploesti • 2nd Lt. Donald Jenkins — Forty Fort, Aircraft: B-24D Lil Joe • 2nd Lt. John T. Ayers — Plymouth, Aircraft: Forky II • S/Sgt. Thomas F. Schappert — Wilkes-Barre, Aircraft: Scrappy II • S/Sgt. James J. Toth — Wilkes-Barre, Aircraft: Maternity Ward • Tech. Sgt. Louis Kase — Hazleton, Aircraft: Ole Kickapoo About the book Makos said the book mentions a fascinating figure from NEPA whose story is largely unknown: Tech. Sgt. Louis Kase of Hazleton. Kase was on the most highly decorated bomber crew in the European Theater during World War II. Makos said Kase was the radio operator of the B-24 Ole Kickapoo — the bomber flying behind the book’s hero, Ernie Poulson, during Operation Tidal Wave. “Kase’s bomber was hit and streaming gasoline, and his pilot did a heroic act earning the Medal of Honor,” Makos said. “Ernie watched Ole Kickapoo crash, killing eight of the 10 crewmen—including Kase. It’s also historic because it’s believed to be the first Medal of Honor captured in a photo.” Here are some stats Makos and his brother, Bryan, found: • 18 men from Pennsylvania died in the raid. • 6 Luzerne County men perished, the most of any county in the state. Two were from Wilkes-Barre and one each from Hazleton, Huntington Mills, Plains Township and Plymouth. The remains of only one — Ayers, 22, of Plymouth — returned here for burial. He was laid to rest in St. Vincent’s Cemetery in Larksville. • Those who died from Luzerne County included Ayers, Schappert, Toth, Kase, Claude Ipher of Huntington Mills, and Jenkins. “I don’t think anyone knows that Kase was on one of the most famous bombers in the greatest raid in Air Force history,” Makos said. Makos said the story follows Lt. Ernie Poulson’s B-24, called Chattanooga Choo Choo, which flew in front of Ole Kickapoo. Makos said it almost reads like a movie script: “In the summer of 1943, every B-24 bomber on that side of the Atlantic was gathered in one place, Benghazi, Libya, to launch a secret mission that could shorten the war dramatically. “By 1943, the Allies understood that Germany could have all the tanks, airplanes, and ships in the world, but without fuel, they couldn’t go anywhere. And Romania was Hitler’s single most important source of petroleum, supplying 30% of his oil. “So, the idea behind Tidal Wave was audacious — send American bombers roughly 2,100 miles round trip from North Africa and destroy the refineries around Ploesti — what the Americans called “Hitler’s Gas Station.” “They were going to come in at treetop level, hoping to achieve surprise and put their bombs directly into the refineries to cripple a vital source of fuel for the German war machine.” Learning about the story Makos said he was actually steered to the story in a most unexpected way. In 2018, he was visiting with Fred Smith, the founder and CEO of FedEx, who was producing a movie about Makos’ book “Devotion.” “But that day in Memphis, he didn’t want to talk about the film project,” Makos said. “Instead, he told me the story behind Tidal Wave — that during the most dramatic air raid of World War II, one bomber was shot down and crash-landed on the estate of a Romanian princess. She was their enemy by nationality, but what she did next would form a bond between her and the American crew that would last the rest of their lives.” Makos said Smith told him if he could write this book and bring the story back to life, then they could make the movie of it. Makos said it was like looking for a needle in a haystack. It was 75 years after the war — any survivor would have to be at least 95. Makos and his brother started digging and found that of the 1,700 men who flew the raid, only one man was still alive: Ernie Poulson. And by chance, Ernie was the co-pilot on the bomber that landed on the princess’s estate. Makos said Poulson was 97, but his memory was still sharp. He’d risen to the rank of colonel in the Air Force and afterward became a professor at the University of Utah. Poulson’s story was amazing — he told of the rookie crew on their second mission when they flew in the Ploesti raid — the worst second mission a crew could ask for. Before they took off, Makos said Ernie made a vow: “If only one plane comes back, we’ll be on it.” On Aug. 1, 1943, American airmen set out for Ploesti. It was enormous — 178 B-24 Liberators and roughly 1,700 airmen from five bomb groups. Makos said they made their low-level attack, but their B-24 was badly damaged. They lost an engine, barely staying in the air, and Ernie and his pilot, Bob O’Reilly, realized they weren’t going home. Now they had one job left — put the dying bomber down without killing everybody aboard. They came down in a riverbed in the Romanian countryside. The B-24 was torn apart, and amazingly, most of the crew survived. “When Ernie was shot down and he made a run for it from his crashed bomber, he was eventually captured and imprisoned in a cistern below ground,” Makos said. That’s where he first met Princess Catherine Caradja, a princess from one of Romania’s oldest families. She had already rescued Ernie’s navigator, extracting him from the damaged aircraft where he was pinned and soaked in gasoline. She owned 1,000 acres, including the land they crashed on. “And Ernie was surprised to discover that she would have been happy not to have another drop of oil reach Hitler,” Makos said. “She didn’t blame them for coming there and bombing the Romanian refineries.” From there, Ernie and 110 other POWs went on to encounter the strangest POW experience of World War II, when he was imprisoned in an Alpine lodge high in the Transylvanian Alps. But Princess Catherine stayed in the picture, visiting the prisoners, bringing them food and supplies, advocating for them — helping them survive captivity so they could one day make it home to their mothers. “This book shares the common theme with my earlier ones — of enemies who become friends, of humanity in wartime,” Makos said. Takeaways from this book Makos hopes readers will come to understand that Ernie and his comrades are important Americans who earned their place in our memory. “They flew arguably the most spectacular mission in military history, and many of them paid for it with their lives — 45 bombers were shot down by enemy fire, a quarter of those that set out,” Makos said. “The casualty rate was the highest of any single air mission in American history.” But, Makos said, so was the valor. “Five Medals of Honor were awarded from this mission, three of them posthumously, which gives you an inkling of the danger the raid entailed — more than even D-Day,” Makos said. “There were 56 Distinguished Service Crosses, our nation’s second-highest award for valor. And 1,700 Distinguished Flying Crosses — one for every man who flew the mission.” And ultimately, Makos said the raid later produced an incredible result. When Hitler’s panzers made their last gamble in the Ardennes, they ran out of gas. German tanks stopped cold in the snow during the Battle of the Bulge because they had run out of fuel. “That result had its origins when Ernie and the guys went barreling toward those refineries in August 1943,” Makos said. “And at the end of the war, new German fighter pilots were going into battle with just 12 hours of flight time in their Me-109s because there wasn’t enough fuel to fly training missions. The Ploesti raiders set that in motion when they bombed seven of the nine refineries.” Epilogue Makos said 310 Americans gave their lives — men like much of the crew of Ole Kickapoo, and they did help bring about an earlier end to the most terrible war in human history. “Are we a country that remembers our heroes, those audacious young men who flew into the jaws of hell?” Makos asked. “Or will they be just a footnote in history? These people are too important to forget. Help bring Ploesti raid back to modern memory.” Local journalism matters, and your support makes it possible.
